subject: English
q: Identify the correct form of the sentence: “You had better to leave before the roads are blocked.”
o: You had better leave before the roads will be blocked.
You had better to leave before the roads are blocked.
You had better leave before the roads are blocked.
You had better leaving before the roads are blocked.
explanation: “Had better” is followed by the bare infinitive; the time clause stays in the present.

subject: English
q: Which version of this sentence is grammatically correct? “I would rather to stay at home than go to the crowded market.”
o: I would rather stay at home than go to the crowded market.
I would rather stay at home than going to the crowded market.
I would rather stay at home then go to the crowded market.
I would rather to stay at home than go to the crowded market.
explanation: “Would rather…than” takes bare infinitives on both sides; “then” is not the comparative word.

subject: English
q: Correct the sentence: “The committee consists from five members of parliament.”
o: The committee is consisting of five members of parliament.
The committee consists from five members of parliament.
The committee consists of five member of parliament.
The committee consists of five members of parliament.
explanation: “Consist” takes “of” and, as a stative verb, is not used in the continuous.

subject: English
q: Choose the error-free version of: “No citizen should be deprived from his basic rights.”
o: No citizen should been deprived of his basic rights.
No citizen should be deprived of his basic rights.
No citizen should be deprive of his basic rights.
No citizen should be deprived from his basic rights.
explanation: “Deprive” takes “of”; after “should” the passive is “be deprived”.

subject: English
q: Identify the correct form of the sentence: “The audience could not help to laugh at the speaker’s joke.”
o: The audience could not helped laughing at the speaker’s joke.
The audience could not help to laugh at the speaker’s joke.
The audience could not help laughing at the speaker’s joke.
The audience could not help laughing on the speaker’s joke.
explanation: “Cannot help” in the sense of “cannot avoid” is followed by a gerund; one laughs “at” something.

subject: English
q: Which version of this sentence is grammatically correct? “The old fort at Rohtas is worth to visit.”
o: The old fort at Rohtas is worth of visiting.
The old fort at Rohtas are worth visiting.
The old fort at Rohtas is worth to visit.
The old fort at Rohtas is worth visiting.
explanation: “Worth” is followed directly by a gerund, without “to” or “of”.

subject: English
q: Correct the sentence: “Seldom we see such dedication in public servants.”
o: Seldom do we see such dedication in public servants.
Seldom do we sees such dedication in public servants.
Seldom do we saw such dedication in public servants.
Seldom we see such dedication in public servants.
explanation: A sentence opening with the negative adverb “seldom” requires inversion (“do we see”); “dedication” here is uncountable.

subject: English
q: Choose the error-free version of: “Not only he writes novels, but he also paints landscapes.”
o: Not only does he writes novels, but he also paints landscapes.
Not only does he write novels, but he also paints landscapes.
Not only he writes novels, but he also paints landscapes.
Not only does he write novels, but he also paint landscapes.
explanation: When “not only” begins a clause, the auxiliary comes before the subject (“does he write”).

subject: English
q: Identify the correct form of the sentence: “She felt badly about missing her friend’s wedding.”
o: She felt bad about miss her friend’s wedding.
She felt badly about missing her friend’s wedding.
She felt bad about missing her friend’s wedding.
She feel bad about missing her friend’s wedding last week.
explanation: “Feel” is a linking verb here, so it takes the adjective “bad”, not the adverb.

subject: English
q: Which version of this sentence is grammatically correct? “Our team played very good in the final.”
o: Our team played very well in the final.
Our team played very well at final.
Our team play very well in the final last year.
Our team played very good in the final.
explanation: An action verb is modified by the adverb “well”, not the adjective “good”.

subject: English
q: Correct the sentence: “A pair of new shoes are lying under the bed.”
o: A pair of new shoes is laying under the bed.
A pairs of new shoes is lying under the bed.
A pair of new shoes are lying under the bed.
A pair of new shoes is lying under the bed.
explanation: The subject is “a pair”, which is singular; “lie” is the verb meaning to rest.

subject: English
q: Choose the error-free version of: “The injured man laid on the road until the ambulance came.”
o: The injured man laid on the road until the ambulance came.
The injured man lay on the road until the ambulance came.
The injured man lay on the road until the ambulance come.
The injured man lied on the road until the ambulance came.
explanation: The past of “lie” (to recline) is “lay”; “laid” is the past of “lay” (to put) and “lied” means told a lie.

subject: English
q: Identify the correct form of the sentence: “Prices of essential goods have raised sharply this month.”
o: Prices of essential goods have rose sharply this month.
Prices of essential goods have raised sharply this month.
Prices of essential goods has risen sharply this month.
Prices of essential goods have risen sharply this month.
explanation: “Rise” is intransitive (prices rise), and its past participle is “risen”; “raise” needs an object.

subject: English
q: Which version of this sentence is grammatically correct? “The murderer was hung after the court rejected his appeal.”
o: The murderer was hanged after the court rejected his appeal.
The murderer was hanged after the court reject his appeal.
The murderer was hung after the court rejected his appeal.
The murderer were hanged after the court rejected his appeal.
explanation: For execution the past participle is “hanged”; “hung” is used for objects such as pictures.

subject: English
q: Correct the sentence: “The teacher was angry on the students for coming late.”
o: The teacher was angry with the students for come late.
The teacher was angry on the students for coming late.
The teacher was angry with the students for coming late.
The teacher were angry with the students for coming late.
explanation: One is angry “with” a person (and “at” or “about” a thing).

subject: English
q: Choose the error-free version of: “The province was divided in six administrative divisions.”
o: The province was divide into six administrative divisions.
The province was divided into six administrative divisions.
The province was divided in six administrative divisions.
The province were divided into six administrative divisions.
explanation: Splitting into parts is expressed by “divide into”.

subject: English
q: Identify the correct form of the sentence: “The students listened the lecture with great attention.”
o: The students listened to the lecture with a great attentions.
The students listen to the lecture with great attention yesterday.
The students listened the lecture with great attention.
The students listened to the lecture with great attention.
explanation: “Listen” needs “to” before its object.

subject: English
q: Which version of this sentence is grammatically correct? “The speaker emphasised on the need for tax reform.”
o: The speaker emphasis the need for tax reform.
The speaker emphasised the need for tax reform.
The speaker emphasised on the need for tax reform.
The speaker emphasise the need for tax reform.
explanation: “Emphasise” is transitive and takes its object directly; only the noun “emphasis” is followed by “on”.

subject: English
q: Correct the sentence: “The boy resembles with his grandfather in many ways.”
o: The boy resembles his grandfather in many ways.
The boy is resembling his grandfather in many ways.
The boy resembles with his grandfather in many ways.
The boy resemble his grandfather in many ways.
explanation: “Resemble” takes a direct object and, as a stative verb, is not normally used in the continuous.

subject: English
q: Choose the error-free version of: “The flood prevented the relief trucks to reach the villages.”
o: The flood prevented the relief trucks to reach the villages.
The flood prevent the relief trucks from reaching the villages last week.
The flood prevented the relief trucks from reaching the villages.
The flood prevented the relief trucks from reach the villages.
explanation: “Prevent” is followed by an object + “from” + gerund.

subject: English
q: Identify the correct form of the sentence: “She succeeded to pass the competitive examination on her first attempt.”
o: She succeeded to pass the competitive examination on her first attempt.
She succeeded in passing the competitive examination on her first attempt.
She succeed in passing the competitive examination on her first attempt.
She succeeded in pass the competitive examination on her first attempt.
explanation: “Succeed” takes “in” followed by a gerund.

subject: English
q: Which version of this sentence is grammatically correct? “The more you practise, more confident you become.”
o: The more you practise, the more confidently you become.
More you practise, the more confident you become.
The more you practise, more confident you become.
The more you practise, the more confident you become.
explanation: The correlative comparison needs “the” in both halves (“the more…the more”); “become” takes the adjective “confident”.

subject: English
q: Correct the sentence: “It was so a hot day that the schools were closed.”
o: It was such a hot day that the schools were closed.
It was such a hot day than the schools were closed.
It was so a hot day that the schools were closed.
It was such hot day that the schools were closed.
explanation: “Such a” is used before an adjective + singular noun (“such a hot day”); “so” goes directly before an adjective.

subject: English
q: Choose the error-free version of: “The box was too heavy that the child could not lift it.”
o: The box was so heavy that the child could not lifted it.
The box was so heavier that the child could not lift it.
The box was so heavy that the child could not lift it.
The box was too heavy that the child could not lift it.
explanation: “Too” is followed by an infinitive (“too heavy to lift”); a “that” clause requires “so”.

subject: English
q: Identify the correct form of the sentence: “He is lonely because he has a few friends in the city.”
o: He is lonely because he has a few friends in the city.
He is lonely because he has few friend in the city.
He is lonely because he has few friends in the city.
He is lonely because he has little friends in the city.
explanation: “Few” (without “a”) means “hardly any” and fits the idea of loneliness; “a few” means “some”, and “little” is for uncountable nouns.

subject: English
q: Which version of this sentence is grammatically correct? “There were not much people at the seminar on Friday.”
o: There were not many people at the seminar in Friday.
There were not many people at the seminar on Friday.
There were not much people at the seminar on Friday.
There was not many people at the seminar on Friday.
explanation: “People” is a countable plural noun and takes “many”.

subject: English
q: Correct the sentence: “These kind of mistakes are common in the first draft.”
o: This kind of mistake is common on the first draft.
This kind of mistake are common in the first draft.
These kind of mistakes are common in the first draft.
This kind of mistake is common in the first draft.
explanation: “Kind” is singular, so it needs “this” and a singular verb; “in a draft” is the correct preposition.

subject: English
q: Choose the error-free version of: “The results are not announced yet by the commission.”
o: The results have not been announced yet by the commission.
The results has not been announced yet by the commission.
The results are not announced yet by the commission.
The results have not been announce yet by the commission.
explanation: “Yet” in a negative sentence goes with the present perfect; the passive is “have been announced”.

subject: English
q: Identify the correct form of the sentence: “The bridge has been built ten years ago.”
o: The bridge was built since ten years.
The bridge has been built ten years ago.
The bridge was build ten years ago.
The bridge was built ten years ago.
explanation: “Ago” marks a finished past time and takes the simple past, not the present perfect.

subject: English
q: Which version of this sentence is grammatically correct? “This time tomorrow we will fly over the Arabian Sea.”
o: This time tomorrow we will flying over the Arabian Sea.
This time tomorrow we will be flying over the Arabian Sea.
This time tomorrow we will be flying on the Arabian Sea.
This time tomorrow we are be flying over the Arabian Sea.
explanation: An action in progress at a particular future moment takes the future continuous “will be flying”.

subject: English
q: Correct the sentence: “The award was give to the best-performing teacher.”
o: The award was give to the best-performing teacher.
The award was gave to the best-performing teacher.
The award was given to the best-performing teacher.
The award were given to the best-performing teacher.
explanation: The passive voice uses “be” + past participle (“was given”).

subject: English
q: Choose the error-free version of: “I will get my car repair before the trip to Swat.”
o: I will have my car repaired before the trip to Swat.
I will have my car repair before the trip to Swat.
I will have my car repaired before the trip for Swat.
I will have repaired my car before the trip to Swat by a mechanic.
explanation: The causative structure for getting something done by someone else is “have + object + past participle”.

subject: English
q: Identify the correct form of the sentence: “The number of road accidents have risen during the holidays.”
o: The number of road accidents has rose during the holidays.
The number of road accidents has risen during the holidays.
The number of road accident has risen during the holidays.
The number of road accidents have risen during the holidays.
explanation: “The number of” is singular and takes “has”; the participle of “rise” is “risen”.

subject: English
q: Which version of this sentence is grammatically correct? “The company announced it’s annual profits on Monday.”
o: The company announced its annual profits on Monday.
The company announced its annual profit’s on Monday.
The company announced it’s annual profits on Monday.
The company announce its annual profits on Monday.
explanation: The possessive form is “its”; “it’s” is a contraction of “it is”.

subject: English
q: Correct the sentence: “We enjoyed very much at the wedding in Lahore.”
o: We enjoyed ourself very much at the wedding in Lahore.
We enjoyed very much at the wedding in Lahore.
We enjoyed ourselves very much at the wedding in Lahore.
We enjoyed us very much at the wedding in Lahore.
explanation: “Enjoy” needs an object; when the meaning is “have a good time”, the reflexive “ourselves” is used.

subject: English
q: Choose the error-free version of: “The prize was shared between he and she.”
o: The prize was shared between he and she.
The prize was shared among him and her.
The prize was shared between him and she.
The prize was shared between him and her.
explanation: After a preposition both pronouns take the object case; “between” is used for two people.

subject: English
q: Identify the correct form of the sentence: “Imran was best student in our class.”
o: Imran was best student in our class.
Imran was the most best student in our class.
Imran was the best students in our class.
Imran was the best student in our class.
explanation: A superlative adjective before a noun takes “the”.

subject: English
q: Which version of this sentence is grammatically correct? “She is a MBA from a well-known business school.”
o: She is a MBA from a well-known business school.
She has an MBA from a well-known business school.
She has an MBA from well-known business school.
She has a MBA from a well-known business school.
explanation: The letter M is pronounced “em”, so it takes “an”; a person has (holds) a degree rather than “is” one, and “school” needs an article.

subject: English
q: Correct the sentence: “The children go to the school by bus every morning.”
o: The children goes to school by bus every morning.
The children go to the school by bus every morning.
The children go to school by bus every morning.
The children go to school with bus every morning.
explanation: When “school” means the institution for its purpose, it takes no article; “by bus” also takes no article.

subject: English
q: Choose the error-free version of: “Scarcely had the meeting begun than the power failed.”
o: Scarcely had the meeting begun when the power failed.
Scarcely had the meeting began when the power failed.
Scarcely had the meeting begun than the power failed.
Scarcely the meeting had begun when the power failed.
explanation: “Scarcely” pairs with “when”, needs inversion and takes the past participle “begun”.

subject: English
q: Identify the correct form of the sentence: “The committee has not decided whether to extend the deadline or no.”
o: The committee has not decided that whether to extend the deadline or not.
The committee has not decide whether to extend the deadline or not.
The committee has not decided whether to extend the deadline or no.
The committee has not decided whether to extend the deadline or not.
explanation: The correct pairing is “whether…or not”.

subject: English
q: Which version of this sentence is grammatically correct? “He talks as if he was the owner of the company.”
o: He talks as if he were the owner of the company.
He talks as if he were the owner of company.
He talk as if he were the owner of the company.
He talks as though if he were the owner of the company.
explanation: An unreal comparison after “as if” takes the subjunctive “were”.

subject: English
q: Correct the sentence: “The new policy neither reduces costs nor it improves service.”
o: The new policy neither reduce costs nor improve service.
The new policy neither reduces costs nor improves service.
The new policy neither reduces costs or improves service.
The new policy neither reduces costs nor it improves service.
explanation: “Neither…nor” should join parallel verbs without repeating the subject; “neither” pairs with “nor”.

subject: English
q: Choose the error-free version of: “His hobbies are reading, travelling and to cook.”
o: His hobbys are reading, travelling and cooking.
His hobbies is reading, travelling and cooking.
His hobbies are reading, travelling and cooking.
His hobbies are reading, travelling and to cook.
explanation: Items in a list should be parallel: three gerunds.

subject: English
q: Identify the correct form of the sentence: “Teaching children to think is more important than to teach them facts.”
o: Teaching children to think is more important than teaching them facts.
Teaching children to think are more important than teaching them facts.
Teaching children to think is more importanter than teaching them facts.
Teaching children to think is more important than to teach them facts.
explanation: The two things compared should be in the same form: “teaching…than teaching”.

subject: English
q: Which version of this sentence is grammatically correct? “Either of these two roads lead to the motorway.”
o: Either of these two roads lead to the motorway.
Either of these two roads leads at the motorway.
Either of these two roads leads to the motorway.
Either of these two road leads to the motorway.
explanation: “Either” (one of two) is singular and takes “leads”.

subject: English
q: Correct the sentence: “Five hundred rupees are not enough for a family meal these days.”
o: Five hundred rupees are not enough for a family meal these days.
Five hundred rupees is not enough for a family meal these days.
Five hundred rupees is not enough to a family meal these days.
Five hundreds rupees is not enough for a family meal these days.
explanation: An amount of money thought of as a single sum takes a singular verb.

subject: English
q: Choose the error-free version of: “The jury were unanimous in its verdict.”
o: The jury was unanimous in it’s verdict.
The jury is unanimous in its verdict yesterday.
The jury were unanimous in its verdict.
The jury was unanimous in its verdict.
explanation: When a collective noun acts as a single unit, as here with “its”, the verb is singular.

subject: English
q: Identify the correct form of the sentence: “Being a rainy day, the match was cancelled.”
o: As it was a rainy day, the match was cancelled.
As it was a rainy day, the match was cancel.
As it was a rainy day, the match cancelled.
Being a rainy day, the match was cancelled.
explanation: The participle phrase “being a rainy day” has no logical subject (the match was not a rainy day); an adverb clause with its own subject fixes it.

subject: English
q: Which version of this sentence is grammatically correct? “He is not enough experienced to lead the department.”
o: He is not enough experienced to lead the department.
He is not experienced enough to lead the department.
He is not experience enough to lead the department.
He is not experienced enough for lead the department.
explanation: “Enough” follows an adjective (“experienced enough”) and is followed by an infinitive.

subject: English
q: Correct the sentence: “She goes always to the library after classes.”
o: She goes always to the library after classes.
She always go to the library after classes.
She always goes to the library after classes.
She always goes to library after classes.
explanation: Adverbs of frequency such as “always” come before the main verb.

subject: English
q: Choose the error-free version of: “I know him since we were at school together.”
o: I know him since we were at school together.
I have knew him since we were at school together.
I have known him for we were at school together.
I have known him since we were at school together.
explanation: A state lasting from a past point until now, with “since”, takes the present perfect “have known”.

subject: English
q: Identify the correct form of the sentence: “Hundreds of trees were fallen to widen the road.”
o: Hundreds of trees were felled to widen the road.
Hundreds of trees were fallen to widen the road.
Hundreds of trees was felled to widen the road.
Hundreds of trees were felled for widen the road.
explanation: “Fell” (to cut down) is transitive and its participle is “felled”; “fall” is intransitive and cannot be passive.

subject: English
q: Which version of this sentence is grammatically correct? “Everybody must bring their own identity card with themselves.”
o: Everybody must bring his or hers own identity card.
Every bodies must bring his or her own identity card.
Everybody must bring his or her own identity card.
Everybody must brings his or her own identity card.
explanation: The correct version uses the singular “his or her” with a singular noun and drops the needless reflexive.

subject: English
q: Correct the sentence: “On medical advice he has stopped to smoke completely.”
o: On medical advice he has stopped to smoke completely.
On medical advice he has stop smoking completely.
On medical advice he have stopped smoking completely.
On medical advice he has stopped smoking completely.
explanation: “Stop smoking” means to give up the habit; “stop to smoke” means to pause in order to smoke.

subject: English
q: Choose the error-free version of: “I don’t like neither of the two proposals.”
o: I likes neither of the two proposals.
I like neither of the two proposals.
I like neither of the two proposal.
I don’t like neither of the two proposals.
explanation: “Neither” is itself negative, so it cannot be combined with “don’t” (alternatively: “I don’t like either”).

subject: English
q: Identify the correct form of the sentence: “The new engine is capable to run on solar power.”
o: The new engine is capable of run on solar power.
The new engine is capable of running on solar power.
The new engine is capable to run on solar power.
The new engine are capable of running on solar power.
explanation: “Capable” is followed by “of” + gerund.

subject: English
q: Which version of this sentence is grammatically correct? “The novel has been translated in several languages.”
o: The novel have been translated into several languages.
The novel has been translate into several languages.
The novel has been translated in several languages.
The novel has been translated into several languages.
explanation: Change from one language to another is expressed by “translate into”.

subject: English
q: Correct the sentence: “The ministry has not replied my letter yet.”
o: The ministry has not replied to my letter already.
The ministry has not reply to my letter yet.
The ministry has not replied to my letter yet.
The ministry has not replied my letter yet.
explanation: “Reply” needs “to” before its object; “yet”, not “already”, is used in negatives.

subject: English
q: Choose the error-free version of: “Here comes the minister and his advisers.”
o: Here come the minister and his advisers.
Here come the minister and his adviser’s.
Here comes the minister and his advisers.
Here come the minister and him advisers.
explanation: In sentences starting with “here”, the verb agrees with the subject that follows; “the minister and his advisers” is plural.

subject: English
q: Identify the correct form of the sentence: “If he had more time, he will learn French.”
o: If he had more time, he would learnt French.
If he has more time, he would learn French.
If he had more time, he will learn French.
If he had more time, he would learn French.
explanation: A second conditional combines the past tense in the “if” clause with “would” + base verb.

subject: English
q: Which version of this sentence is grammatically correct? “The majority of voters in the constituency is women.”
o: The majority of voters in the constituency are women.
The majority of voters in the constituency is women.
The majority of voters in the constituency are woman.
The majority of voter in the constituency are women.
explanation: When “majority” refers to a number of individuals, as here, it takes a plural verb.
